title: Enhanced Rock Weathering and Organic Inputs: Coupled Controls on Soil Carbon Storage
content:
Enhanced rock weathering in managed soils interacts with externally added and plant-derived organic inputs, reshaping both organic and inorganic carbon pools. These bidirectional interactions can stabilize or destabilize soil carbon, so the net climate benefit of ERW depends on the balance among coupled carbon pathways.


ABSTRACT

Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) is increasingly promoted as a nature-based climate solution that can remove atmospheric CO2. Silicate weathering converts CO2 into dissolved inorganic carbon (IC), primarily bicarbonate, which may subsequently contribute to pedogenic carbonate formation. Although ERW does not produce organic C (OC), it may influence the persistence or loss of native or newly introduced OC. Yet the mechanisms governing coupled IC and OC storage remain poorly constrained. In this review, we synthesize emerging evidence from modern agricultural and other managed-soil studies on how ERW alters soil OC (SOC) and soil IC (SIC) dynamics by modifying mineral surface reactivity, organic matter turnover, and soil chemistry. Evidence to date indicates that ERW can alter SOC through several linked abiotic and biotic pathways. Increased reactive mineral surface area, divalent-cation availability, and aggregation can promote mineral association and physical protection of OC, whereas changes in pH, microbial activity, and mineral reactivity can also enhance OC decomposition or destabilize existing organo-mineral interactions. Accordingly, ERW effects on SOC remain variable across rock types, soils, application rates, and timescales. Organic inputs from amendments and living plants can further modify these responses, but available studies show no consistent effect of organic-input source on SOC storage. Most studies do not distinguish native from externally applied or plant-derived OC nor resolve transitions among free particulate OC, occluded particulate OC, dissolved OC, and mineral-associated OC. The climate benefit of ERW depends on the coupled response of inorganic and organic C pools, and on how soil properties, mineralogy, and organic inputs shape their balance over time. Resolving these interactions is essential for assessing the long-term C sequestration potential of ERW-based strategies across diverse soil systems.
